points: This nevuah came on Tisha B'Av, in the seventh year of Yechezkel's exile. The Abarbanel notes that from the fifth year on, Yechezkel delivered one major prophecy each year - and this one's date, Tisha B'Av, foreshadows the churban that would arrive on that same day a few years later.

The elders who come are called Ziknei Yisrael, which the commentators read as the unrighteous elders, in contrast to Ziknei Yehuda. They come 'seeking God,' and Hashem refuses to answer them. The Radak explains: they wanted explanations and clarity about what would happen, not change. We turn to Hashem ultimately to change ourselves, so their request is rejected and replaced with a directive about how to live.

The chapter reveals something the Chumash never records: in Mitzrayim the Jews were warned not to serve idols - the Rishonim bring a tradition that Aharon was a navi there - and they did not listen. Rashi says this is why most of the people died during the plague of darkness: 'vachamushim alu' means only a fifth left Mitzrayim, while four-fifths had assimilated into Egyptian culture.

The chapter traces a pattern: rebellion in Mitzrayim, rebellion in the desert even after receiving the Torah, idolatry in Eretz Yisrael. Each time Hashem holds back destruction not because the people deserve it, but because we are called by His name - once we are God's people, whatever happens to us, good or bad, reflects on Him. Our fate is never only about us.

In exile the people despair: we are finished, we will simply become like the nations. Hashem answers: no - I will rule over you even with fury rather than let you disappear. And the message lands with us: even an incomplete return to Eretz Yisrael can serve as an impetus, a catalyst for us to change as well.
